intro: Each object begins with a different material and skill. The modern visitor makes the carved surfaces and featherwork easier to compare at human scale.
alt: Microsoft looks at carved Māori wood, a Sepik carved fragment, a Rapa Nui stone sculpture study and a red-and-yellow Hawaiian feather cloak.

variants.name: Māori carving
variants.look: Curving ridges throw fine shadows, and small areas of shell reflect light against the reddish wood.
variants.history: Māori whakairo includes practices of carving wood and other materials. Carved figures on meeting houses and objects can express connections with particular ancestors and communities.
variants.when: Study attributed examples for the way a carved piece relates to its place in a larger structure.
variants.why: Depth and repeated curves let an architectural design carry across a wall or a room.

source.label: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

variants.name: Sepik carving
variants.look: Elongated lines and incised surfaces make the wooden fragment visually distinct from its display mount.
variants.history: Many different peoples live along Papua New Guinea's Sepik River and have distinct carving traditions. Some forms belong to ceremonial houses or other community settings.
variants.when: Study an identified carving alongside details about its use and original setting.
variants.why: An object that seems narrow or abstract in a case may have made sense as part of architecture or performance.

variants.name: Rapa Nui art
variants.look: A heavy brow, long nose and broad shoulders stand out in the stone profile.
variants.history: Rapa Nui communities carved moai from stone and set many on ceremonial platforms. The island's art also includes wood carving and other forms.
variants.when: Study a documented moai when you want to understand how very large sculpture works in relation to land and ancestry.
variants.why: Simplified features hold their place against the horizon and remain distinct at a distance.

variants.name: Hawaiian featherwork
variants.look: Fine red and yellow feathers make broad crescents that stay bright across the cloak's curved surface.
variants.history: Specialists made Hawaiian feather cloaks called ʻahu ʻula by attaching bundles of feathers to netting. The garments signaled high rank and held political and ceremonial significance.
variants.when: Look at how tiny units of material make a clear form both near the body and from afar.
variants.why: Light catches many overlapping feathers while the large color bands preserve the outline of the design.

She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space.
